scenes.text: Last time, we said adults can't just guess what health means to young people. So, let's find out. Suppose you want to know what health means to students at your school. Write the one question you'd ask them. Now test it. Could two people give opposite answers, and both be telling the truth? Could someone answer it in three words? And would they be comfortable if their answer were read out in class with their name on it?

Most weak investigations fail before any data is collected, because the question can't be answered. Four tests catch most problems. Can you collect data to answer it? Is it specific about who and what? Is it neutral, or does it lead people to an answer? And would different answers actually be interesting? "Why do young people ignore their mental health?" fails, because it's decided they do. Try, "What do Year 11 students at this school say health means to them?"

The syllabus names three methods, and each one buys something different. A survey reaches lots of people quickly, but its options are written in advance, so for a question about meaning, the options become the answer. An interview can follow up a surprising answer and ask why, but it's slow, so the sample is small. A semi-structured interview uses a set list of questions, with room to follow up. A focus group shows how views form when people hear each other, but louder voices dominate, and people hold back in front of peers. For meanings, a strong design is mixed: a short open survey to find the range, then interviews to understand a few in depth.

Next, be honest about who you actually asked. Your sample is the people who answered. The population is everyone you want to describe. They're not the same. If a student surveys her own basketball team about fitness and health, she's learned about her team, not about young people. And volunteers aren't random either. The students most interested in health are the most likely to sign up, which pushes the answers in a direction you can name.

Research about health asks people about their bodies, their families and sometimes their worst weeks, so ethics matters as much here as in a university study. People give informed consent, knowing what's involved and that they can stop, and under eighteen that usually means a parent or guardian too. Taking part must be truly voluntary, which is harder when the researcher is a friend or a captain. Decide whether you're offering anonymity or confidentiality, and say which. Plan for distress, and know where to send someone for support. Research with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people needs community consultation and control. And report everything you found, including the answers that spoil your pattern.

The requirement students most often miss is the right to withdraw, including withdrawing answers they've already given. Here's the catch. A truly anonymous survey makes that impossible, because you can't find whose answers to remove. That's not a flaw, but you must tell people before they answer. And never promise anonymity on a survey that asks for a name and a class.

Now, can your data be trusted? Three separate questions. Validity: did you measure what you meant to measure? Counting how often students exercise doesn't tell you what health means to them. Reliability: would you get the same result again? If interviewers word questions differently, answers move for the wrong reasons. Credibility: can you trust the source, who collected it, and what did they stand to gain? These are independent. A study can be reliable and still measure the wrong thing.

A finding is what your data shows. A conclusion is what you're entitled to say because of it. "Eleven of twenty-four students described health as keeping up with what their day demands" is a finding. "Young people define health functionally" is a much bigger claim than twenty-four students can support. Next, read differences as patterned. If students from one part of town answer differently, that's not noise. The determinants change what health has cost them. Finally, name a question your findings raised but couldn't answer.

Three questions for any data. Validity: did you measure the right thing? Reliability: would you get it again? Credibility: can you trust the source? And a conclusion can only be as big as the finding behind it.

Two exam questions. First. A class runs the same health-meanings survey twice, once in the week after exams and once in a normal week, and gets very different results. Identify whether this mainly damages validity, reliability or credibility, and propose a repair. Pause here to answer.

Mainly reliability: run twice, it didn't give the same result. You could also argue validity, because the post-exam week added a condition unrelated to what health means to them. Either way, the repair is to run both at comparable times, with the same instructions. The classic mistake is calling it credibility, but nothing about the source changed.
Second. Justify the choice of method for an investigation into the meanings of health for young people. Pause here to answer.

The question needs meanings in people's own words. So choose semi-structured interviews, which can ask why. Then reject the alternatives with reasons. A fixed survey can't return a meaning nobody wrote down, and a focus group can hide private views. Concede the cost, a small sample, and reduce it with a short open survey first. The classic mistake is praising your method without saying why the others fit worse.

So, a trustworthy investigation runs the whole cycle: a sharp question, a method that fits it, an honest sample, ethics built in, checks on validity, reliability and credibility, and conclusions no bigger than the findings. National health reports run the same cycle on a huge scale, and their first finding about young people is surprising. Next, we'll see why reports still worry about the healthiest age group.
